Encourage your kids to learn to cook from a young age.

When my husband and I were dating we visited a family that had started going to our church. They had 11 or 12 kids at the time, I think they have 14 now. Their eight year old daughter knew more about managing a home and cooking than I did at 19.

Yes! They are so much more capable then people think.
My 5 year old can make scrambled eggs and french toast with supervision. She has helped make her own pb&js since she was 2. She also brushes the bread with butter and garlic for garlic bread.
My almost 3 year old helps with what she can too.

Yes! Grandma plopped my butt on a high stool and had me stirring pots and mixing batter by the time I was 4. I As a latch-key kid I was able to feed myself pretty well when my parents weren't home. And I used to make a little extra cash by delivering homage "pizza" (made with canned biscuit dough crust) and fried "elephant ears" to neighborhood kids. I was making simple dinners for my family by myself by age 8. Now I can cook or bake just about anything and I can easily create my own recipes without a cookbook. I do mess things up once in a while (especially if it's one of my "experiments") but it's been years since I had anything turn out inedible.

Being a good cook allowed me to save a lot of money in our poorer years, really stretch the grocery budget, and make the most of limited money to create really great meals and desserts for special occasions. I also used to cook for everyone on the family vacations instead of payin our full share of the rental fee (we couldn't have afforded it and would have had to stay home). Everyone else was happy to pay a little more and save money on eating out.

These days I can spend a little more on groceries and entertain guests with really great meals. Or take something awesome to the bake sale. Or make a really extravagant cake or dessert.

Good cooking skills have also allowed me to cope with a variety of cooking challenges. No power for a week? No problem. I know how to light a gas stove when the power is out, or I can cook on a charcoal grill, a wood fire, a camp stove, or even the top of a space heater or a candle! Can't drive to the store for whatever reason for a few days? I know what to substitute and how to pull a meal together from whatever is on hand. Currently my refrigerator is broken (broke 2 weeks ago). It's another week till the new one is delivered, I have 4 cubic feet of refrigerator space available to me. I'm making some amazing stuff from canned, dried, and shelf stable food.

My inlaws can barely boil water. Their kids have often talked about how much they loved auntie lastditchtryforaname's cooking over the years (which has actually caused a few hurt feelings to their moms) And several of them have come to me over the years to learn some cooking basics.

Cooking is a basic life skill. Teach it to your some and daughters as early as you can.
